why: An increasing price triplet is an increasing subsequence of length 3, and we maximise the profit sum instead of the length: a weighted LIS capped at 3. Fix the middle day j, and you need the best profit to its left with a smaller price and the best to its right with a larger price.
hints: Fix the middle day j. What do you need from the days before it and the days after it?
For each j: left[j] = max profit[i] over i < j with price[i] < price[j], right[j] = max profit[k] over k > j with price[k] > price[j]. The answer is the max of left[j] + profit[j] + right[j].

Compute left with a prefix-max Fenwick tree over compressed prices (query ranks strictly below, then insert), and right with a second one scanning from the end over mirrored ranks. O(n log n) time; an O(n^2) double loop also works for small n.
pitfalls: Strictly increasing prices: equal prices cannot be used together, so query ranks strictly less (or greater).
If no triplet exists, return -1, and do not let a missing left or right side be treated as 0.
Use a true minus-infinity sentinel if profits may be negative.
constraints:
• 1 <= n <= 10^5, price.length == profit.length == n
  • 1 <= price[i], profit[i] <= 10^9
  • Not stated in the source; reasonable bounds for an O(n log n) solution.
